### The sliding quarterback and the defenseless player

When a quarterback runs, he becomes a runner and can be tackled like one, with one exception. If
he **slides feet first**, he is giving himself up: the ball is dead the instant he touches the ground
with anything but his hands or feet, and defenders must treat him like a runner already
[down by contact](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-down-by-contact) (down because an opponent touched
him, the subject of the next chapter) and pull up. "Pull up" has a limit that decides most late-slide
arguments on a broadcast: a defender who had already committed to the tackle before the slide began
isn't flagged for contact he couldn't avoid, unless he hits the quarterback in the head or neck with
his helmet, shoulder or forearm, or does something else needlessly rough. The rule also puts the
burden on the quarterback: slide early, before a hit is imminent, or lose the protection. A
quarterback who *fakes* a slide is treated as having slid (the ball is dead
when he begins the fake), so he can't use it to freeze a defender and keep running. The current rule
treats a dive, feet or head first, the same way as a slide.[^slide]

The **[defenseless player](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-defenseless-player)** rule generalises
the idea. The rule book lists players who can't protect themselves: a passer in the act of throwing
or just after; a receiver trying to catch a pass (and until he has had time to protect himself after
the catch); a runner already held up with his
[forward progress](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-forward-progress) stopped (his advance halted, so
the play is effectively over); a kicker or punter during the
kick; a kick returner fielding the ball; a quarterback after a change of possession; a player on the
ground; a player hit by an illegal **blindside block** (a block thrown while the blocker is moving
toward or parallel to his own end line, with forcible contact from the helmet, forearm or shoulder;
itself 15 yards); a receiver running his route when the defender
comes from the side or behind; and a few others. Against them a
defender may not make forcible contact to the head or neck with the helmet, face mask, shoulder or
forearm, and may not **launch** (leave his feet and spring upward and forward into the player). The
foul is **[unnecessary roughness](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-unnecessary-roughness)**, the
catch-all personal foul that also covers late hits after the whistle and hits on players out of
bounds: **15 yards**, with an automatic first down when the defense commits it.[^defenseless]

The defenseless-player rule is why you see safeties aiming low, at a receiver's thighs, on a pass
over the middle instead of "lighting him up" high. It is a rule that changed how a position is played.

### The 2018 helmet rule

In 2018 the NFL went further with the **[use of the helmet (2018 rule)](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-use-of-the-helmet-2018-rule)**:
it is a foul for **any player, anywhere on the field**, to lower his head to initiate and make contact
with his helmet against an opponent. Unlike the defenseless-player rules, it covers runners and
blockers as well as tacklers, and it applies to everyone on every play, not just to hits on certain
players. The penalty is **15 yards**, and a flagrant violation can be an ejection.[^helmet]

### Tackles that are banned: the horse-collar and the hip-drop

Two tackles are illegal by name:

- **[Horse-collar tackle](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-horse-collar-tackle)** (banned in 2005).
  Grabbing the inside back or side collar of a runner's shoulder pads or jersey and pulling him down,
  usually from behind. The runner's legs fold under him as he falls backward, which breaks ankles and
  tears knee ligaments. The ban followed the 2004 season, in which Dallas safety Roy Williams's
  horse-collar tackles injured several players, among them Philadelphia's Terrell Owens.[^horsecollar]
  15 yards and an automatic first down.
- **[Hip-drop tackle](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hip-drop-tackle)** (banned in 2024). The
  tackler wraps the runner from behind or the side, swings his hips and legs off the ground, and drops
  his weight onto the runner's legs at or below the knee. The league's injury data showed the
  technique injuring runners at a far higher rate than ordinary tackles, and the owners banned it in
  March 2024, unanimously and over the objections of the players' union, with a 15-yard penalty and an automatic
  first down.[^hipdrop]

### Discipline beyond the flag: the 2026 three-strike policy

A flag is only one price. Players are also fined, and the worst hits bring suspensions. For the
2026 season the league and the players' union agreed on a **three-strike policy** for five listed
fouls (hip-drop tackles, horse-collar tackles, launching, hits on a defenseless player, and blindside
blocks): three violations bring a one-game suspension, and the strikes carry over into later seasons.
Everyone started the 2026 regular season with a clean slate. Reports differ on one detail: the
Associated Press describes three violations across the categories, while ProFootballTalk reads the
policy as three violations of the *same* rule. Strikes come from the league's discipline after
review, not only from flags.[^threestrike]
The point is to reach the habits that flags and fines hadn't changed, especially for the hip-drop,
which is rarely flagged (below).

| Rule | Since | What it bans | Price on the field | Why it was written |
|:--------------------|:------:|:----------------------|:--------------|:----------------------|
| Horse-collar tackle | 2005 | Pulling a runner down by the back or side collar | 15 yd + 1st down | Leg and ankle injuries from runners folded backward |
| Low hit on the passer ("Brady rule") | 2009 | Forcible hits at or below a passer's knees | 15 yd + 1st down | Knee injuries to quarterbacks |
| Chop block (all situations) | 2016 | High-low double blocks | 15 yd | Knee injuries to linemen |
| Use of the helmet | 2018 | Lowering the head to initiate helmet contact, anyone, anywhere | 15 yd, possible ejection | Head and neck injuries to both players |
| Roughing: body weight emphasis | 2018 | Landing on the passer with most of the body weight | 15 yd + 1st down | Shoulder and collarbone injuries to quarterbacks |
| Hip-drop tackle | 2024 | Swinging the hips onto a runner's legs | 15 yd + 1st down | Lower-leg injuries to runners |
| Three-strike policy | 2026 | Repeat violations of five listed safety rules | One-game suspension after three | Repeat offenders flags didn't deter |

: The main player-safety rules and when they arrived. Personal fouls by the defense carry an automatic first down; flagrant ones can bring an ejection. Sources in the footnotes to this section. {#tbl-safety}

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists: safety rules with a scheme side effect"}
**What they solve.** Head, neck and knee injuries that a career, or a life, can't recover from.
**What they change.** Defensive backs tackle lower and play the ball instead of the man; rushers
learn to hit the quarterback's torso and roll off him; offenses gain yards on every borderline call,
and a quarterback who slides gets a free end to his run. Each rule also creates a judgment call, and
judgment calls on 15-yard fouls swing games. That tension, between protecting players and leaving
the officials too much to decide, runs through every live rules debate.
:::

## How a flag becomes yards: enforcement

Now the mechanics. When a flag flies during a play, the officials answer a fixed sequence of
questions. Learn them and you can usually announce the result before the referee does.

### Accept or decline

Most fouls happen during a live play, and the play keeps going until it ends normally. Then the team
that was fouled gets a choice: **[accept or decline](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-accept-decline-penalty)**.
Accept, and the result of the play is usually wiped out and the penalty enforced. Decline, and the
play stands as though no foul happened.[^enforce] In practice the head coach decides, quickly, with
the referee explaining the options to the team captain or the coach on the sideline.

The choice is usually obvious (nobody declines a 40-yard DPI) but not always:

- **Third down, incomplete pass, offensive holding.** Accept, and it's third-and-18 from ten yards
  back. Decline, and it's fourth-and-8: the offense will probably punt. Most defenses decline,
  because a stop now beats a long third down later. In 2021–2025 offenses converted third-and-16
  to third-and-20 about `{python} f"{CONV_3L:.0%}"` of the time; a declined penalty that forces the
  punt takes even that chance away.
- **Defensive offside on a touchdown pass.** The offense declines and keeps the touchdown. A
  defensive *personal foul* on a touchdown isn't lost, though: the rules carry it over to the try,
  so the offense can kick the extra point from closer or go for two from the 1. (A personal foul on
  a successful extra-point kick can be carried to the kickoff instead.)
- **A sack and a hold.** If the offense held and the quarterback was sacked anyway for 9 yards, the
  defense can take the sack (and the down) or the 10 yards (and replay the down), whichever leaves
  the offense worse off.
- **Two fouls by the same team** on one play don't add up. The fouled team picks the one it wants
  enforced, and the other is dropped.
- **Fouls by both teams** on the same play usually **offset**: the penalties cancel and the down is
  replayed.

Some fouls aren't part of the choice in the usual way. Fouls *after* the play is over (a late hit, a
taunt, a fight) are **dead-ball fouls**: the play's result stands and the yardage is added on, from
where the play ended. That's how a 20-yard completion plus a late hit becomes 35 yards.[^td-fouls]

### Free plays

**[Free play](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-free-play)** is the accept-or-decline option seen
from the other end, and [The Pre-Snap Phase](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd) showed
it in action. When a defender is offside at the snap, the play goes on with the flag already down.
The offense can't lose: if the play works, it declines the penalty and keeps the result; if it fails
(incomplete, sacked, even intercepted), it takes the five yards. So quarterbacks are taught to snap
fast and take a shot downfield.

The catch is that not every jump gives a free play. If a defender's jump makes a nearby blocker
flinch, or leaves him with an unblocked path to the quarterback, the officials blow the whistle at
once: a **neutral zone infraction**, five yards, no play (encroachment if he touches someone). The
free play happens when the jumper draws no reaction and isn't running free, typically a wide end who
jumps and is picked up by his tackle, or a twelfth defender still running off the field at the snap
([What a Play Really Is](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd)). That's also why the
quarterback snaps it *fast* on a jump: the play has to start before anybody reacts.[^nzi]

```{python}
#| label: fig-free-play
#| fig-cap: "A free play, simulated (BDB-format tracking generated by gridiron). Set: the left defensive end (E) is in his stance outside the left tackle. Snap: he has jumped into the neutral zone (dashed outline: where he was), but nobody flinched and the tackle is in front of him, so there is no whistle; the center snaps the ball before he can get back, he is offside, and the flag comes out while the play runs. The quarterback, knowing the offense can take five yards if this goes badly, throws deep to X against the press corner, a throw he would rarely risk on a normal second down. If X catches it, the offense declines the flag; if it falls incomplete or is intercepted, the offense accepts it and replays the down five yards closer. Had the tackle flinched, or had the end been running free at the quarterback, the officials would have blown it dead before the snap: a neutral zone infraction."
def free_play():
    off = offense("gun_2x2")
    dfn = defense("nickel", "single_high", off, press=True)
    dfn = [q.moved(label="C") if q.pos == "CB" else q for q in dfn]
    dfn = [q.moved(d=13.5, w=0.0) if q.key == "FS" else q.moved(d=2.5, w=-9.2) if q.key == "SS" else q for q in dfn]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
    p.motion("WDE", to=(-0.2, -4.7), speed=2.4)                 # the jump: into the neutral zone
    p.route("X", r.go(32)); p.route("H", r.hitch(6)); p.route("Y", r.hitch(6)); p.route("Z", r.curl(12))
    p.dropback(2.5)
    p.pass_to("X", t=1.7)
    for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
        p.block(k, pts=[(-1.0, 0.0)])
    for k in ("SDE", "SDT", "WDT"):
        p.rush(k, pts=[(-1.6, 0.0)], speed=2.0)
    p.rush("WDE", pts=[(-1.6, 0.4)], speed=2.0)
    p.man("LCB", "X"); p.man("NB", "Y"); p.man("RCB", "Z"); p.man("SS", "H")
    p.drop("FS", (20.0, -6.0), speed=6.0)
    p.drop("MIKE", (6.0, 1.0)); p.drop("WILL", (6.0, -4.0))
    p.highlight("WDE", "X")
    return p


fp = free_play()
FP_T = [-1.2, 0.0, 1.7, 3.4]
FP_LAB = ["Set", "Snap \u00b7 E offside", "+1.7 s \u00b7 the shot", "+3.4 s \u00b7 free play"]
if PDF:
    VIEWS = [((-13, 6.5), (-7, 8.5)), ((-13, 6.5), (-7, 8.5)), ((-21, 5), (-9.5, 31)), ((-21, 5), (-9.5, 31))]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(6.6, 2.75))
    per = {0: dict(notes=[(5.9, -8.4, "E set outside\nthe tackle", dict(fs=5.4))]),
           1: dict(flags=[(-4.4, -9.6)],
                   notes=[(5.5, -8.4, "jumps into the\nneutral zone: flag,\nplay goes on", dict(fs=5.4, color=FOUL))]),
           2: dict(flags=[(-6.2, -11.0)]),
           3: dict(flags=[(-6.2, -11.0)],
                   notes=[(24.0, -6.4, "caught: decline\nthe flag. Missed\nor picked: take\n5 yards", dict(fs=5.4))])}
    for i, (ax, t, lab, (lat, win)) in enumerate(zip(axes, FP_T, FP_LAB, VIEWS)):
        fld = snapshot(fp, t, ax, lat, win, **per.get(i, {}))
        if i >= 1:                                              # where the end was set
            x0, y0 = P_(fld, fp, 1.0, -5.0)
            ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x0 - 0.75, y0 - 0.75), 1.5, 1.5, fc="none", ec=style.DEFENSE_DARK,
                                   lw=0.8, ls=(0, (2, 1.2)), zorder=7))
        if i == 1:
            arrow(fld, fp, (1.55, -5.75), (0.35, -5.75), FOUL, lw=1.1, ms=7, z=9)
        panel_title(ax, lab, fs=8.0)
    fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.5)
    plt.show()
else:
    show_animation(fp, times=FP_T)
```

### From which spot, and how far

If the penalty is accepted, the officials need a starting point and a distance:

- **The previous spot** (where the ball was snapped) is the default for most fouls, including all
  pre-snap fouls, every foul during a pass play (offensive holding, offensive pass interference,
  defensive holding, illegal contact), and every offensive foul behind the line of scrimmage.
- **The spot of the foul** is used for defensive pass interference (the spot foul) and for many
  offensive fouls on running plays and returns: a block in the back 20 yards upfield on a punt
  return is walked off from where it happened.
- **The end of the play** is used for dead-ball fouls after the whistle, and is an option for a
  defensive personal foul such as roughing the passer on a completed pass (the offense gets
  whichever of the previous spot and the end of the play helps it more).

The middle bullet is the one fans get wrong, and it has a logic. On a run, the officials compare the
foul with the **end of the run**. A hold that happens *behind* that point, but past the line, is
walked off from the spot of the foul: the offense keeps the yards it gained up to the hold, which
came before the foul could help, and loses everything after it plus ten yards. A hold *beyond*
where the run ended couldn't have helped the runner, so it is walked off from the end of the run,
and the offense keeps the whole gain before paying ten yards. A hold behind the line of scrimmage
goes back to the previous spot, as on a pass.[^runenf] The NFL calls this the *three-and-one*
method; you only need the picture.

```{python}
#| label: fig-run-enforce
#| fig-cap: "Offensive holding on a run, three ways (offense moving right). First-and-10 at the offense's own 30; the back runs to the 42. Top: a receiver holds a corner at the 38, past the line but behind where the run ended, so ten yards come off from the spot of the foul: first-and-12 at the 28. Middle: the hold is at the 46, beyond where the run ended; it couldn't have helped the runner, so the ten yards come off the end of the run: first-and-8 at the 32. Bottom: a lineman holds behind the line, at the 28, so the penalty goes back to the previous spot: first-and-20 at the 20."
def yard_strip(ax, lo, hi, prev, half=6.75, num_w=-4.9):
    """A horizontal strip of field from yard line lo to hi (offense's own territory, moving right)."""
    los = 10 + prev
    f = Field(ax=ax, orient="horizontal", los=los, window=(10 + lo - los, 10 + hi - los),
              lateral=(FIELD_W / 2 - half, FIELD_W / 2 + half), to_go=None, numbers=False)
    p = Play([O_("Q", "QB", 0.0, 0.0, "")], [], los=los, ball_y=FIELD_W / 2, to_go=None)
    for yl in range(lo - lo % 10 + 10, hi, 10):
        say(f, p, yl - prev, num_w, str(yl) if yl else "G", color=style.MUTED, fs=7.5, weight="bold")
    return f, p


def run_row(ax, foul, end, new_spot, tag, note, from_spot):
    f, p = yard_strip(ax, 8, 56, 30, half=5.4, num_w=-3.8)
    line_across(f, p, 0.0, style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=1.6, ls="-", w0=-5.4, w1=5.4)
    line_across(f, p, 10.0, style.LINE_TO_GAIN, lw=1.6, ls="-", w0=-5.4, w1=5.4)
    arrow(f, p, (0.0, 0.2), (end - 30, 0.2), style.OFFENSE, lw=1.6, ms=8)          # the run
    ball(f, p, end - 30, 0.2)
    star(f, p, foul - 30, -1.5, FOUL, ms=11)
    say(f, p, foul - 30 + 1.4, -1.5, note, fs=6.2, color=FOUL, ha="left", box=False)
    arrow(f, p, (from_spot - 30, 2.0), (new_spot - 30, 2.0), FOUL, lw=1.6, ms=8)
    x0, y0 = P_(f, p, new_spot - 30, 0.0)
    ax.plot([x0, x0], [y0 - 2.8, y0 + 2.8], color=FOUL, lw=1.8, zorder=6)
    say(f, p, (from_spot + new_spot) / 2 - 30, 3.7, tag, fs=6.6, color=FOUL, weight="bold")
    return f


fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(6.5, 4.5))
run_row(axes[0], 38, 42, 28, "from the spot of the foul: 1st-and-12", "hold", 38)
run_row(axes[1], 46, 42, 32, "from the end of the run: 1st-and-8", "hold", 42)
run_row(axes[2], 28, 42, 20, "from the previous spot: 1st-and-20", "hold", 30)
for ax, t in zip(axes, ["1. Hold behind the end of the run, past the line",
                        "2. Hold beyond the end of the run",
                        "3. Hold behind the line of scrimmage"]):
    panel_title(ax, t, fs=8.2)
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

Then **how far**: five, ten or fifteen yards, or the spot. And then two adjustments near the goal
lines:

- **[Half the distance](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-half-the-distance).** A penalty may not
  move the ball more than halfway to the offending team's goal line. Holding by the offense on its
  own 8 moves the ball to the 4, not to the end zone. A defensive personal foul with the ball on the
  opponent's 6 moves it to the 3. Without the rule, a penalty could score points; with it, the ball
  keeps creeping toward the goal line but never gets there.[^halfdist]
- **Fouls in the end zone.** Offensive holding in the offense's own end zone is a **safety**: the
  spot the penalty would be walked from is already behind the goal line, so instead of moving the
  ball the rules give the defense two points. DPI in the end zone puts the ball on the 1, not in the
  end zone. The rule book awards a touchdown for a foul only in the rare case of a *palpably unfair
  act* (a player coming off the bench to tackle a runner headed for the end zone, say), and pass
  interference, however blatant, isn't one.[^palpably]

```{python}
#| label: fig-half-distance
#| fig-cap: "The same offensive holding call, ten yards, at three spots near the offense's own goal line (offense moving right). Top: from the 35 the full 10 yards apply, so the next snap is at the 25. Middle: from the 8, ten yards would carry the ball into the end zone, so it moves half the distance to the goal line, to the 4. Bottom: the ball is snapped from the 2 and the quarterback drops back into his own end zone; a hold there, four yards deep, is a safety: two points to the defense, and the offense must free-kick."
def strip_row(ax, prev, new_spot, tag):
    f, p = yard_strip(ax, -9, 42, prev)
    say(f, p, -5 - prev, -4.9, "end zone", color=style.INK_2, fs=6.8, style_="italic", box=False)
    line_across(f, p, 0.0, style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=1.6, ls="-", w0=-6.7, w1=6.7)
    ball(f, p, 0.0, 0.0)
    arrow(f, p, (0.0, 2.6), (new_spot - prev, 2.6), FOUL, lw=1.6, ms=9)
    ball(f, p, new_spot - prev, 0.0)
    x0, y0 = P_(f, p, new_spot - prev, 0.0)
    ax.plot([x0, x0], [y0 - 3.4, y0 + 3.4], color=FOUL, lw=1.6, zorder=6)
    say(f, p, (new_spot - prev) / 2, 4.6, tag, fs=7.0, color=FOUL, weight="bold")
    return f


fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(6.5, 4.6))
strip_row(axes[0], 35, 25, "10 yd")
strip_row(axes[1], 8, 4, "4 yd")
f, p = yard_strip(axes[2], -9, 42, 2)
say(f, p, -7.0, -4.9, "end zone", color=style.INK_2, fs=6.8, style_="italic", box=False)
line_across(f, p, 0.0, style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=1.6, ls="-", w0=-6.7, w1=6.7)
ball(f, p, 0.0, 0.0)
arrow(f, p, (-0.3, 0.0), (-5.3, 0.0), style.OFFENSE, lw=1.3, ms=7)
draw_marker(axes[2], *P_(f, p, -6.0, 0.0), "off", "Q", f.pts_per_yard())
star(f, p, -6.0, 2.0, FOUL, ms=11)
flag(f, p, -3.4, 3.4, s=1.1)
say(f, p, 9.5, 2.6, "hold in his own end zone: safety", fs=7.0, color=FOUL, weight="bold")
for ax, t in zip(axes, ["1. Holding with the ball on the 35: the full 10 yards, to the 25",
                        "2. Holding on the 8: half the distance to the goal line, to the 4",
                        "3. Snap from the 2, hold in his own end zone: a safety"]):
    panel_title(ax, t, fs=8.2)
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

### What down is it?

Last question: the down.

- **Fouls by the offense** usually **replay the down**: second-and-10 becomes second-and-20 after a
  hold. A few also cost a down (an illegal forward pass, intentional grounding; see
  [Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball](09-04-officiating-replay-and-rules-of-the-ball.qmd)).
- **Fouls by the defense** come in two kinds. The pre-snap and procedural fouls (offside,
  encroachment, neutral zone infraction, too many men) replay the down unless the yards reach the line
  to gain. The contact and safety fouls (defensive holding, illegal contact, DPI, roughing the passer,
  unnecessary roughness and the other personal fouls, illegal hands to the face) carry an
  **automatic first down**, however short the yardage.
- **A half can't end on an accepted defensive foul during a play.** If time runs out on a play
  with a defensive foul and the offense accepts, it gets one untimed down.

```{python}
#| label: fig-flag-flow
#| fig-cap: "What happens when a flag flies: the officials' sequence, and yours. Answer the five questions in order and you can announce the result before the referee does."
steps = [
    ("1  When?", "Before the snap with a whistle (false start, encroachment, neutral zone infraction: no play)? During the play, including offside at the snap (a live-ball foul: the play runs)? Or after it ended (a dead-ball foul: late hit, taunt; the play stands)?"),
    ("2  Who?", "Offense or defense? If both, the fouls usually offset and the down is replayed."),
    ("3  Accept/decline?", "The fouled team compares the play's result with the penalty's result and keeps the better one."),
    ("4  Where, how far?", "Previous spot (pass plays, pre-snap fouls, offense fouls behind the line), spot of the foul (DPI; offense fouls past the line but behind the end of a run, and on returns), or end of the play (dead-ball fouls; offense fouls beyond the end of a run); 5, 10, 15 yards or the spot; half the distance near a goal line."),
    ("5  What down?", "Offense foul: replay the down (a few cost one). Defense contact or personal foul: automatic first down. Defense procedural foul: replay unless the yards reach the sticks."),
]
wrapped = ["\n".join(textwrap.wrap(body, 66)) for _, body in steps]
heights = [1.9 + 0.95 * (w.count("\n") + 1) for w in wrapped]      # 1 unit = 0.155 in
gap = 0.9
total = sum(heights) + gap * (len(steps) - 1)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 0.155 * total))
ax.set_xlim(0, 100); ax.set_ylim(0, total); ax.axis("off")
y1 = total
for i, ((head, _), body, h) in enumerate(zip(steps, wrapped, heights)):
    y0 = y1 - h
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((1, y0 + 0.15), 98, h - 0.3, boxstyle="round,pad=0.15,rounding_size=0.6",
                                fc=style.SURFACE if i % 2 else style.OFFENSE_TINT, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=0.9))
    ax.text(3.5, (y0 + y1) / 2, head, fontsize=8.6, fontweight="bold", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, va="center")
    ax.text(32, (y0 + y1) / 2, body, fontsize=7.4, color=style.INK, va="center", linespacing=1.2)
    if i < len(steps) - 1:
        ax.annotate("", xy=(14, y0 - gap + 0.05), xytext=(14, y0 + 0.05),
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=style.INK_2, lw=1.0))
    y1 = y0 - gap
plt.show()
```

## What penalties cost {#what-penalties-cost}

Now price them. Every NFL game has about `{python} f"{ALL_FLAGS.loc[2025]:.0f}"` fouls named in the
play-by-play (both teams, accepted or declined, in 2025), and a handful of types account for most of
them.

```{python}
#| label: fig-penalty-rates
#| fig-cap: "Flags per game (both teams) for eight common fouls, 2015-2025 regular seasons. Offensive holding and false starts are the two most common by far. Holding dropped sharply in 2020, when officials were told to call it less, and has since climbed back. Roughing the passer peaked in 2018-2021 after the body-weight emphasis and fell back from 2022. Illegal contact jumps around from year to year, as emphasis changes. Source: nflverse play-by-play, one foul per play (the play's main foul), accepted or declined, all plays including kicks; each panel has its own scale."
SHOW = [("Offensive Holding", "Offensive holding"), ("False Start", "False start"),
        ("Defensive Pass Interference", "Def. pass interference"), ("Defensive Holding", "Defensive holding"),
        ("Unnecessary Roughness", "Unnecessary roughness"), ("Roughing the Passer", "Roughing the passer"),
        ("Illegal Contact", "Illegal contact"), ("Offensive Pass Interference", "Off. pass interference")]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(6.6, 3.7), sharex=True)
yrs = RATES.index.values
for ax, (col, name) in zip(axes.flat, SHOW):
    v = RATES[col].values
    ax.plot(yrs, v, color=style.SERIES[0], lw=1.8, marker="o", ms=2.6)
    ax.set_ylim(0, max(v) * 1.3)
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=7.4, loc="left")
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=6.6)
    ax.set_xticks([2015, 2020, 2025])
    ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
    ax.text(yrs[-1] + 0.3, v[-1], f"{v[-1]:.2f}", fontsize=6.4, color=style.INK, va="center")
    ax.set_xlim(2014.5, 2027.2)
    if col == "Offensive Holding":
        ax.annotate("2020", xy=(2020, RATES.loc[2020, col]), xytext=(2016.2, RATES.loc[2020, col] * 0.55),
                    fontsize=6.4, color=style.INK_2, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=style.INK_2, lw=0.7))
for ax in axes[:, 0]:
    ax.set_ylabel("flags per game", fontsize=6.8)
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.9, w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

How often a foul is called is half the story. The other half is what each one is worth. Because
nflverse computes expected points before and after every snap, a penalty snap gets an EPA like any
other: the value of the down, distance and yard line after the flag, minus the value before. (That
includes the play the flag wiped out, which is gone; the EPA reflects only where the penalty left the
ball.) Averaging by foul type gives a price list in points.

```{python}
#| label: fig-penalty-epa
#| fig-cap: "The average swing in expected points (EPA, from the offense's point of view) when a foul is accepted, 2021-2025 regular seasons, scrimmage downs. Fouls by the defense (orange) help the offense; fouls by the offense (blue) hurt it. The number on each bar is the average penalty yardage. Illegal use of hands, face mask and unnecessary roughness can be committed by either side, so each appears twice, once per side (only cases with at least 40 accepted flags are shown). Source: nflverse play-by-play."
ORDER = ["Roughing the Passer", "Defensive Pass Interference", "Unnecessary Roughness", "Illegal Contact",
         "Defensive Holding", "Face Mask", "Neutral Zone Infraction", "Defensive Offside", "Illegal Use of Hands",
         "False Start", "Ineligible Downfield Pass", "Illegal Block Above the Waist", "Offensive Holding",
         "Offensive Pass Interference"]
NAMES = {"Illegal Use of Hands": "Hands to the face", "Illegal Block Above the Waist": "Block in the back",
         "Ineligible Downfield Pass": "Illegal man downfield", "Defensive Offside": "Offside (defense)",
         "Roughing the Passer": "Roughing the passer", "Defensive Pass Interference": "Defensive pass interference",
         "Unnecessary Roughness": "Unnecessary roughness", "Illegal Contact": "Illegal contact",
         "Defensive Holding": "Defensive holding", "Face Mask": "Face mask", "Neutral Zone Infraction": "Neutral zone infraction",
         "False Start": "False start", "Offensive Holding": "Offensive holding",
         "Offensive Pass Interference": "Offensive pass interference"}
MIXED = {"Illegal Use of Hands", "Face Mask", "Unnecessary Roughness"}
e = EPA_S.reset_index()
e = e[e.penalty_type.isin(ORDER) & (e.n >= 40)]
e = e[e.penalty_type.isin(MIXED) | (e.by_off == (e.penalty_type.map(EPA_T.by_off) > 0.5))].sort_values("epa")
labels = [NAMES[t] + ((" (offense)" if bo else " (defense)") if t in MIXED else "") for t, bo in zip(e.penalty_type, e.by_off)]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.6))
cols = [style.OFFENSE if bo else style.DEFENSE for bo in e.by_off]
ax.barh(labels, e.epa, color=cols, height=0.66)
for i, (ep, yd) in enumerate(zip(e.epa, e.yds)):
    ax.text(ep + (0.04 if ep >= 0 else -0.04), i, f"{ep:+.2f}  ({yd:.0f} yd)", va="center",
            ha="left" if ep >= 0 else "right", fontsize=7.2, color=style.INK)
ax.axvline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1.0)
ax.set_xlim(e.epa.min() - 0.75, e.epa.max() + 0.75)
ax.set_xlabel("Average EPA for the offense when the foul is accepted", fontsize=8)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7.4)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.legend(handles=[Patch(color=style.DEFENSE, label="foul by the defense"), Patch(color=style.OFFENSE, label="foul by the offense")],
          loc="lower right", fontsize=7.5)
plt.show()
```

Four things stand out.

1. **The automatic first down is worth more than the yards.** Defensive holding and illegal contact
   are five-yard fouls, the same yardage as a false start, yet they swing about a point toward the
   offense while a false start costs about two-thirds of one the other way. Splitting the two-sided
   fouls by team shows the same thing: hands to the face is worth more against the defense (five
   yards and a first down) than offside is (five yards, no first down).
2. **DPI and roughing the passer cost a defense more than a completed pass usually gains.** The
   average completion in these seasons was worth about `{python} f"{COMP_EPA:+.2f}"` EPA; a DPI flag
   averaged `{python} f"{EPA_T.loc['Defensive Pass Interference', 'epa']:+.2f}"`, and roughing
   `{python} f"{EPA_T.loc['Roughing the Passer', 'epa']:+.2f}"`.
3. **Offensive holding is a drive-killer.** At about `{python} f"{EPA_T.loc['Offensive Holding', 'epa']:+.2f}"`
   EPA, a hold costs a little over half of what a sack does (`{python} f"{SACK_EPA:+.2f}"` on average), and
   holds are flagged about two and a half times a game.
4. **The same five-yard foul is worth more on later downs.** The table shows it.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bydown
#| tbl-cap: "The same five-yard defensive foul (defensive holding or illegal contact, accepted) by down, 2021-2025 regular seasons. Each carries an automatic first down, so its value rises as the down gets later: on third down it erases a likely punt. Source: nflverse play-by-play."
t = BYDOWN.reset_index()
t = pd.DataFrame({"Down": t["down"].astype(int).map({1: "1st", 2: "2nd", 3: "3rd", 4: "4th"}),
                  "Flags": t["n"].map(lambda v: f"{v:,}"),
                  "Average yards to go": t["togo"].map(lambda v: f"{v:.1f}"),
                  "Average EPA for the offense": t["epa"].map(lambda v: f"{v:+.2f}")})
md_table(t)
```

On first-and-10 a defensive hold is a modest gain, first-and-5. On third-and-7 it erases a likely
punt and hands the offense a fresh set of downs, so it's worth about three times as much. That's why
defensive coordinators preach discipline on third down above all, and why an offense with a long
third down will often throw toward the corner it thinks is most likely to grab.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper: penalties in EPA work"}
Analysts don't agree on how to treat penalty snaps. The usual "EPA per play" leaves out snaps that a
penalty wiped out (nflverse marks them `play_type == "no_play"`), which drops most DPI flags and most
holding calls from team numbers. [Expected Points and Success Rate](../13-analytics-and-data/13-02-expected-points-and-success-rate.qmd)
shows how much that choice shades run-versus-pass comparisons; the DPI flags alone make passing look
a little better once they are counted. For your own work: say which choice you made, and remember
that nflverse records one foul per play, so a play with two flags carries only one penalty type.

Labels move, too. The 2018 helmet foul appears in nflverse under its own name, "lowering the head
to initiate contact," at about 0.07 to 0.13 flags a game from 2018 to 2020, then fades in 2021 and
vanishes from the labels after that.[^helmet-data] Whether those calls dried up or are now filed
under another name (unnecessary roughness is the likely home), the series breaks there. Check a
category's history before you chart it.
:::

## The rules keep moving: live debates

Every spring the competition committee and the teams propose rule changes, and the owners vote; a
change needs 24 of 32 votes. The rules in this chapter will keep changing, so here are the debates
that were live going into the 2026 season. (For how these fit the long history of rule changes,
see [The 1978 Liberation](../11-history/11-02-the-1978-liberation.qmd) and
[Dynasties and Counterpunches](../11-history/11-04-dynasties-and-counterpunches.qmd); for the
timeline, [Appendix E](../../appendices/appendix-e-rules-timeline-trees.qmd).)

- **The tush push.** The [tush push](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tush-push) is a quarterback
  sneak with teammates shoving the quarterback from behind, the Eagles' near-automatic short-yardage
  play ([Red Zone, Goal Line, Two-Point Plays, and Short Yardage](../10-situational-football/10-03-red-zone-goal-line-and-short-yardage.qmd)
  explains it). Pushing the runner has been legal since the NFL removed its ban in 2005; *pulling*
  him (a teammate grabbing his arm or jersey and hauling him forward) is still a foul, ten yards, and
  it's the one to watch for in a tush-push pile. In 2025 Green
  Bay proposed banning it again; the proposal was tabled in the spring and a revised version **failed
  22–10 on May 21, 2025**, two votes short of 24. The league tightened its officiating guidance on false
  starts and alignment instead. For 2026, **no team proposed a ban**, and the play is legal this
  season.[^tush] The argument is about safety (a pile of linemen driving forward), about fairness (is
  a nearly unstoppable play bad for the game?) and about whether one team's mastery of a play is a
  reason to outlaw it. The case study is
  [The Eagles: Trenches, RPOs, and the Tush Push](../12-case-studies/12-06-eagles-trenches-and-tush-push.qmd).
- **Is the hip-drop ban being enforced?** The tackle was banned in 2024, but on-field flags have been
  extremely rare: nflverse's play-by-play records `{python} f"{int(HIP.get(2024, 0))}"` hip-drop flag
  in the 2024 regular season and `{python} f"{int(HIP.get(2025, 0))}"` in 2025. The technique happens
  in a blur, from behind, in a pile, which is hard for an official to see live. The league has
  leaned on fines after the game instead, and the 2026 three-strike policy adds suspensions on top.
  Whether discipline after the fact changes behaviour as much as flags would is the open question.
- **Replay for judgment calls.** After the 2019 pass-interference experiment failed, the NFL moved
  more carefully. Since 2025 replay assist may help the referee on objective facts and may
  **overturn** flags for hits on a defenseless player, face mask (grabbing and twisting or pulling
  the face mask), horse-collar, tripping (using a leg to trip an opponent) and roughing or running
  into the kicker (hitting a punter or kicker after the kick). It **cannot add** a foul that wasn't called, and roughing the passer and
  pass interference are not on the list. In 2026 league officials may also be consulted on ejections
  for flagrant acts.[^replay] Proposals for a full "sky judge" who could call fouls from the booth
  keep coming back.
- **College versus NFL.** The college game caps DPI at 15 yards, gives linemen three yards
  downfield instead of one, and treats targeting (a forcible hit to the head) with automatic
  ejections. College offensive pass interference was cut from 15 yards to 10 for 2026.[^ncaa2026]
  Each difference is a live argument for moving the NFL rule toward college, or the reverse; the full
  side-by-side table is in [Appendix E](../../appendices/appendix-e-rules-timeline-trees.qmd) and the
  history in [The College Laboratory](../11-history/11-03-the-college-laboratory.qmd).

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it on Sunday: the flag predictor"}
Every time a yellow flag flies, play referee before the referee does. Say your answers out loud,
then check them against the announcement.

- **Where did the flag come from?** The official's position is a clue. A flag from deep
  downfield (the side judges, field judge or back judge) is usually pass interference, illegal
  contact or defensive holding. A flag from the officials at the line of scrimmage or behind the
  offense is usually holding, a false start or a foul on the quarterback. A flag thrown late, after
  the play, is usually a personal foul. (Who stands where is in
  [Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball](09-04-officiating-replay-and-rules-of-the-ball.qmd).)
- **Was the ball in the air?** If a receiver was grabbed before the throw, guess holding or illegal
  contact (five yards, first down). After the throw, guess DPI and estimate the spot.
- **Accept or decline?** Ask what the fouled team gave up on the play, and whether the next down
  (a punt down, say) already punishes the offense more than the yards would.
- **Enforce it.** Which spot, how far, half the distance near a goal line, and what down. Say the new
  down and distance.
- **Free play?** If a defender jumped and the ball was snapped anyway, watch the quarterback take
  his shot.
- **Keep score.** By the end of a game you'll be calling most flags right. For a running tally,
  log the penalties' expected-points cost from the chart in
  [What penalties cost](#what-penalties-cost): which team gave away more points in flags?
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: backed up, and a flag"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-backed-up
#| fig-cap: "First-and-10 at the offense's own 4. The back runs left and is tackled at the 10, a 6-yard gain. On the backside, the defensive end beat the right tackle inside, and the tackle grabbed him a yard behind the line of scrimmage (the star): flag, offensive holding."
off = offense("i_form")
dfn = defense("4-3_over", "single_high", off)
dfn = [q.moved(d=11.0) if q.key == "FS" else q for q in dfn]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=14, to_go=10)
p.run("RB", [(3.0, -4.2), (6.4, -7.0), (13.0, -8.2)])
p.handoff("RB", t=0.8)
for k, pts in (("LT", [(0.8, -1.0)]), ("LG", [(0.8, -1.0)]), ("C", [(0.8, -1.0)]), ("RG", [(0.8, -1.0)]),
               ("Y", [(0.6, -0.8)]), ("FB", [(3.6, -4.4)])):
    p.block(k, pts=pts)
p.path("SDE", [(-2.5, -1.7)])
p.block("RT", pts=[(-0.7, -0.5)])
p.highlight("RT", "SDE")
f = p.draw(lateral=(-17, 17), window=(-9.5, 14), width_in=5.4)
no_numbers(f.ax)
star(f, p, -1.75, 2.35, FOUL, ms=12)
flag(f, p, -3.4, 6.8, s=1.1)
say(f, p, -5.8, 10.2, "RT holds the end about\na yard behind the line", fs=6.6, color=FOUL)
f.ax.plot(*zip(P_(f, p, -4.9, 8.4), P_(f, p, -2.2, 3.0)), color=style.INK_2, lw=0.6, zorder=8)
say(f, p, 8.6, -11.8, "tackled at the 10", fs=6.6)
say(f, p, -7.4, -9.5, "own end zone", fs=6.6, style_="italic", color=style.INK_2)
plt.show()
```

**The defense has the choice. Does it accept or decline? If it accepts, where does the ball go and
what are the down and distance? Then two variations: what if the tackle had held the end in the end
zone, and what if a receiver had held a defender at the 9, five yards downfield?**
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Accept.** Declining leaves the run standing: second-and-4 at the 10. Accepting is far worse for
the offense:

- **Which spot?** The hold was behind the line of scrimmage, so it goes back to the **previous
  spot**, the 4, even though this was a running play.
- **How far?** Ten yards from the 4 would put the ball in the end zone, so it moves **half the
  distance** to the goal line: to the **2**.
- **What down?** An offensive foul replays the down, and the line to gain stays at the 14:
  **first-and-12 from the 2**, with the offense now one more mistake from a safety and likely to punt
  from its own end zone.

**Variation 1, the hold in the end zone:** an offensive foul behind the offense's own goal line is a
**safety** if the defense accepts: two points and the ball back on a free kick. The defense takes it.

**Variation 2, a receiver's hold at the 9:** that's past the line but behind where the run ended (the
10), so it is walked off from the **spot of the foul**, the 9. Ten yards would be more than half the
distance, so the ball goes halfway, to the 4½: **first-and-9½**. The offense keeps the five yards it
gained before the hold, which is the logic of the run rule, and the defense would probably still
accept, since it beats second-and-4 at the 10.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: the last snap"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-hail
#| fig-cap: "Fourth quarter, 0:04 left, the offense trails by 5 with the ball at the opponent's 42 and no timeouts. Five receivers spread out; the defense rushes three and drops eight, the deepest three at the goal line and in the end zone."
off = offense("gun_empty")
dfn = [D_("E1", "DE", 1.0, -3.6, "E"), D_("T1", "DT", 1.0, 0.0, "T"), D_("E2", "DE", 1.0, 3.6, "E"),
       D_("LCB", "CB", 9.0, -16.5, "C"), D_("RCB", "CB", 9.0, 16.5, "C"), D_("NB", "NB", 15.0, -9.0, "$"),
       D_("DB", "DB", 15.0, 9.0, "D"), D_("MIKE", "MIKE", 10.0, 0.0, "M"), D_("FS", "FS", 40.5, -6.0, "FS"),
       D_("SS", "SS", 40.5, 6.0, "SS"), D_("DB2", "DB", 44.0, 0.0, "D")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=68, to_go=None)
p.highlight("FS", "SS", "DB2")
f = p.draw(lateral="full", window=(-6.5, 49.5), width_in=4.6)
no_numbers(f.ax)
say(f, p, 46.0, -14.0, "end zone", fs=6.8, style_="italic")
line_across(f, p, 42.0, style.INK_2, lw=1.4, ls="-", w0=-26.7, w1=26.7, z=2.4)
say(f, p, 42.0, 15.5, "goal line, 42 yards away", fs=6.4)
plt.show()
```

**What will the offense try, where will the ball be thrown, and why there rather than ten yards
short, where a receiver might be open?**
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A [Hail Mary](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hail-mary) into the end zone**: a long, high
throw to a crowd of receivers, hoping one of them comes down with it. With four seconds left there is
time for one play, and only a touchdown wins, so a completion short of the goal line ends the game as
soon as the receiver is tackled. That is the main reason to throw into the end zone.

The rules add a bonus, and it comes from this chapter: **a half can't end on an accepted defensive
foul.** Pass interference anywhere gives the offense an untimed down at the spot, and the deeper the
foul, the better that down: interference in the end zone puts the ball on the **1-yard line**, a far
better chance than any heave. It cuts the other way too. A half *can* end on an offensive foul, and
any score on that play doesn't count, so a receiver who shoves a defender to get to the ball has
just ended the game. That's why receivers are coached to box out for position, not push.[^lastplay]

That's why the receivers converge on one spot and fight for position, and why defensive backs are
coached to go for the ball (jump and bat it down) rather than for the receiver. Officials are
reluctant to call interference in a crowd where everyone is jostling for a jump ball, but a defender
who grabs or tackles a receiver before the ball arrives gives the offense its best chance of the
day. The eight deep defenders are there to make sure nobody catches it *and* that nobody has to
foul to prevent it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: bunch on third-and-3"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-bunch
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-3 at midfield. The offense lines up in a tight bunch to the right. The defense shows press man coverage on all three bunch receivers (the ringed defenders, each a yard off the ball), with one deep safety."
off = offense("gun_bunch")
off = [q.moved(w=9.0) if q.key == "H" else q.moved(d=-1.2, w=7.2) if q.key == "Y" else
       q.moved(d=-1.2, w=10.8) if q.key == "Z" else q for q in off]
dfn = defense("nickel", "single_high", off, press=True)
mv = {"RCB": (1.0, 11.2), "NB": (1.0, 9.0), "SS": (1.0, 7.1), "LCB": (1.0, -16.6), "SDE": (1.0, 4.0)}
dfn = [q.moved(d=mv[q.key][0], w=mv[q.key][1]) if q.key in mv else q for q in dfn]
dfn = [q.moved(d=4.5, w=2.2) if q.key == "MIKE" else q for q in dfn]
dfn = [q.moved(label="C") if q.pos == "CB" else q for q in dfn]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=60, to_go=3)
p.highlight("SS", "NB", "RCB")
f = p.draw(lateral=(-20, 16), window=(-7.5, 16), width_in=5.4)
no_numbers(f.ax)
say(f, p, 8.6, 10.0, "three defenders pressed\non a tight bunch", fs=6.6)
plt.show()
```

**What kind of route combination should the offense call here? Where must the contact happen for
it to be legal? And what could the defense have done differently before the snap?**
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A rub (pick) concept out of the bunch.** Against press man, with three defenders lined up a yard
off three receivers standing close together, the receivers' release paths will cross the defenders'
paths almost at once. A classic call is one receiver releasing inside on a slant or in-breaking
route, another breaking out to the flat, and the third pushing vertically to clear the area; one of
the defenders chasing his man has to fight through a teammate's release.

**Legal if the contact happens within a yard of the line, or if the receiver just runs his route.**
Because the defenders are pressed, the crossing happens right at the line, inside the one-yard strip
where pass interference can't occur, so even a deliberate bump is legal there. (The rule says *more
than* one yard, so contact at the line or a step past it is safe; officials judge it by eye at full
speed, which is why offenses aim for contact at the line rather than at the edge of the strip.)
Deeper than that, a receiver who keeps running his route and lets a defender run into him is still
legal; one who runs three yards, stops and steps into a defender's path has blocked him, and that is
offensive pass interference, ten yards.

**What the defense could have done:** not press all three. Against bunches, defenses usually
**align at different depths** (one defender pressed, the others four or five yards off), so nobody
can be picked within the first yard; or they **switch/banjo**, trading receivers by agreement so no
defender chases through the traffic; or they play **zone**, where nobody is chasing a man at all.
Lining up pressed on a tight bunch is inviting the rub.
:::

## Takeaways

- **The rule book is a price list, and teams shop.** Five yards, ten, fifteen, the spot, a first
  down, a safety, an ejection: every foul has a price, and coaches decide when it's worth paying (the
  beaten corner's grab, the beaten tackle's hold, the deep throw hunting a flag).
- **A receiver's rules change with depth and with the throw.** Inside five yards, jam him. Past five,
  hands off until the ball is in the air (illegal contact, defensive holding: five yards and a first
  down). After the throw, play the ball (DPI: a spot foul in the NFL, 15 yards in college). The
  offense's restrictions start at the snap: deliberate picks are legal only inside the first yard,
  and beyond it the receiver must not start the contact.
- **The spot foul shapes offense.** Because DPI has no cap in the NFL, deep throws into tight coverage
  carry a hidden bonus, and big receivers who win 50-50 balls or draw flags are worth more.
- **Blocking is about the frame.** Hands inside the chest plate that push and steer are legal;
  grabbing that materially restricts a defender (usually a hand outside the frame), hands to the face,
  blocks in the back, cuts outside the tight end box and chop blocks are not. Holding is usually the
  most-called foul and the most sensitive to officiating emphasis.
- **Safety rules are expensive and contested.** Roughing the passer, the defenseless player, the
  2018 helmet rule, the horse-collar and hip-drop bans are mostly 15-yard personal fouls with an
  automatic first down; from 2026, repeat violations of five listed rules bring a suspension.
- **Enforce it yourself:** accept or decline, which spot (previous spot for passes and anything
  behind the line; on runs, compare the foul with where the run ended), how far (half the distance
  near a goal line), what down. The automatic first down, not the yardage, is what makes a five-yard
  defensive foul worth a point.

[^rub-rule]: NFL, *2026 Official Playing Rules*, Rule 8, Section 5, Article 1 ("any act by a player more than one yard beyond the line of scrimmage [that] significantly hinders an eligible player's opportunity to catch the ball"; "Acts that do not occur more than one yard beyond the line of scrimmage are not pass interference but could be offensive or defensive holding"), Article 2(g) ("Initiating contact with an opponent by shoving or pushing off, thus creating separation") and Article 4(a) ("Blocking more than one yard beyond the line of scrimmage by an offensive player clearly prior to a pass being thrown"): https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/ . The rule makes the offensive foul an *act* by the receiver (a push-off or a block), which is why a receiver who runs his route and is run into has not fouled; NFL Football Operations' video rulebook entry on offensive pass interference shows the distinction: https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-video-rulebook/

[^screens]: NFL, *2026 Official Playing Rules*, Rule 8, Section 5, Article 1 (pass interference can occur on any forward pass thrown from behind the line, "regardless of … whether it crosses the line"), Article 4(a) (blocking more than a yard downfield "clearly prior to a pass being thrown" is offensive pass interference), and Rule 8, Section 3, Article 1, Item 1(b) (an ineligible player who made contact within a yard of the line may, after breaking contact more than a yard downfield, remain "stationary, [move] laterally, or [move] toward his own goal line until a forward pass is thrown"): https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/ . On screen blockers waiting for the throw: Jimmy Kempski, PhillyVoice, "Lack of discipline, and not just drops, Eagles receivers killing big plays" (Nov. 29, 2016), quoting Rule 8-5-4 and describing Green Bay receivers who "get in the way of the Eagles' defensive backs without contacting them, and then once the ball is complete, they engage": https://phillyvoice.com/lack-discipline-and-not-just-drops-eagles-receivers-killing-big-plays . College rules "clearly cover only forward passes that travel beyond the neutral zone": "Pass interference," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pass_interference ; the three-yard college limit is in the note to the college rule (see the footnote on 2026 college changes below).

[^flagrant]: NFL, *2026 Official Playing Rules*, preface ("'Flagrant' … is meant to indicate that the degree of a violation of the rules—usually a personal foul or unnecessary roughness—is extremely objectionable, conspicuous, unnecessary, avoidable, or gratuitous"), Rule 12, Section 2 (personal fouls, each with "disqualification if flagrant"), and the 2026 change to Rule 19, Section 2 permitting league personnel to consult with on-field officials on disqualifications for flagrant football and non-football acts: https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/

[^td-fouls]: NFL, *2026 Official Playing Rules*, Rule 14, Section 2, Article 3 (a personal or unsportsmanlike foul during a touchdown is enforced on the try; on a successful try kick, a foul by the defense may be enforced on the succeeding free kick), Rule 14, Section 1, Article 3 (multiple fouls by one team: "only one penalty may be enforced," at the offended team's choice) and Rule 3, Section 13 (a dead-ball foul "occurs in the continuing action after a down ends"): https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/

[^nzi]: NFL, *2026 Official Playing Rules*, Rule 7, Section 4, Article 4 (neutral zone infraction, whistle immediately: a defender in the neutral zone "with an unimpeded path to the quarterback," or one whose entry causes an offensive player in close proximity "to react (move) immediately"; no foul if there is no reaction and he gets back before the snap) and Article 3 (encroachment: contact before the snap): https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/

[^runenf]: NFL, *2026 Official Playing Rules*, Rule 14, Section 3, Articles 5 and 6 (the basic spot for a running play is where it ended; "If the offense fouls behind the basic spot, enforcement is from the spot of the foul"; an offensive foul in advance of the basic spot is enforced from the basic spot; "Fouls committed by the offense behind the line of scrimmage are enforced from the previous spot"; and an offensive foul behind its own goal line is a safety): https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/

[^palpably]: NFL, *2026 Official Playing Rules*, Rule 11, Section 2, Article 1(e) ("The Referee awards a touchdown to a team that has been denied one by a palpably unfair act") and Rule 12, Section 3, Article 4 (palpably unfair acts); the end-zone DPI enforcement is Rule 8, Section 5 (first down on the 1): https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/

[^lastplay]: NFL, *2026 Official Playing Rules*, Rule 4, Section 8, Article 2 (a period is extended by an untimed down for an accepted live-ball foul by the defense; "If there is a foul by the offense, there shall be no extension of the period. If the foul occurs on the last play of the half, a score by the offense is not counted"): https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/
